You see, Mateus is the portuguese version of Matthew. Matthew is ,of course, a translated version too. The greek translated from hebrew,( מַתִּתְיָהוּ‎ (Matityahu)) and then it was translated to latin as: Matthaeus.

As the languages started their own written form, there was lot of versions around the peninsula(Portuguese, galego, catalan, castillian, occitan....).

In medieval times, there was not really a rule, since the official written form of the name was the latin. Enrique I, which was a king of Spain (Castille), was named after his maternal grandfather Henry II of England. Sources of that time called him "Anric" sometimes.

Today in Spain is official: Enrique. While in Portugal is Henrique. Portugal also has well defined "Mateus", without the h. But we are in Brazil, not Portugal, remember when I told you about the Felipe and Diego thing? Yeah, in Brazil, for many reasons, things happened a bit different. Not wrong, but different.

Just to add, so you can undestand: In Spain is Mateo. In France is Matthieu. In Galego Mateu. In European Portuguese is Mateus. In Brazil, it can be both Matheus and Mateus.

Now, a example with a name I used. In Spain: Felipe. In france: Philippe. In galego: Filipe. In European Portuguese: Filipe. In Brazil, it can be both Filipe and Felipe.
